questions.question: Which artifacts form the core production tokenizer contract?
options: Only the tokenizer vocabulary and cache TTL
Tokenizer rules and IDs, special-token map, template, model checkpoint, and their immutable versions
Only the model checkpoint and GPU driver
Load-balancer configuration and request logs
questions.explanation: The model interprets integer IDs and structural tokens according to its training contract. The tokenizer, special-token mapping, template, and checkpoint therefore have to ship and roll back together.

questions.question: A slice receives 2,000 requests per second with 400 average tokens per request. What offered token work should capacity planning begin with?
options: 5 tokens per second
80,000 tokens per second
400,000 tokens per second
800,000 tokens per second
questions.explanation: Offered token work is request rate multiplied by average tokens per request: 2,000 x 400 = 800,000 tokens per second.

questions.question: Why must a micro-batch have a maximum wait as well as a maximum size?
options: Under light traffic, waiting to fill a large batch can consume the latency budget
A maximum wait changes the tokenizer vocabulary
It guarantees every batch has identical token lengths
It prevents all queue saturation
questions.explanation: Batching shares fixed work, but requests still wait for compatible peers. A time bound prevents efficiency goals from creating unbounded or surprising latency.

questions.question: Which cache key is safe for reusable tokenization results?
options: A hash of text alone
The tokenizer display name and text length
Input hash plus immutable bundle fingerprint, encode options, length policy, offset contract, and required tenant scope
The model name without a revision
questions.explanation: Every input that changes IDs, masks, offsets, truncation, or reuse authorization belongs in the key. A text-only hash can return results from an incompatible contract.

questions.question: A candidate saves 8% of tokens but changes the IDs produced by golden fixtures. What should the release gate do?
options: Promote because average cost improved
Block the release until the contract change is paired with a compatible trained model and approved evidence
Increase canary traffic to hide sample noise
Clear the cache and ignore the mismatch
questions.explanation: Existing token IDs select learned embedding rows. Unexpected ID drift is an exact compatibility failure that an average efficiency gain cannot offset.

questions.question: Queue length rises because long document jobs share workers with interactive chat. What is the best first design response?
options: Remove all input limits
Use one unbounded batch for both workloads
Scale only from HTTP request count
Separate service classes, bound queue age, and scale using measured token work
questions.explanation: Long and short requests have different cost and latency contracts. Isolation, admission bounds, and token-aware signals protect interactive traffic.

questions.question: Which response is appropriate when the requested tokenizer bundle is not loaded and no exact compatible fallback is ready?
options: Silently use the newest tokenizer
Return IDs from a tokenizer with a similar vocabulary size
Fail readiness or return an explicit service-unavailable response
Drop special tokens and continue
questions.explanation: Routing to a different vocabulary can silently corrupt model inputs. The system should fail explicitly until the requested compatible bundle is ready.

questions.question: Which metric best exposes tokenization pressure hidden by request-rate averages?
options: Token work and queue age broken down by bundle and traffic slice
Total HTTP requests without input length
Container uptime alone
The number of tokenizer files in the image
questions.explanation: Token work captures input size while queue age captures waiting impact. Breaking both down by bundle and slice reveals expensive multilingual, code, or document traffic.
